By modulating the gate voltage, we were able to determine the charge occupancy of the nanowires and observed them to have significant energy spacing of approximately 160 meV, which is comparable to their Josephson energy. As a result, the excess energy from quantum phase slips far exceeds the expected energy compared to the tiny Josephson currents, thus rendering their occurrence unlikely. Consequently, our findings suggest that coherent quantum phase slips are unlikely and that the behavior of these nanowires can be explained by the Coulomb blockade instead.

Our proposed approach tackles the challenge of novel view video prediction, taking input from multiple viewpoints. Unlike existing research that relies on narrow angle variations, our network can generate videos from significantly wider angles, up to 45 degrees, without the need for prior knowledge. By processing only RGB frames, we've developed a two-component representation, combining local and global features that enables novel view prediction. Our model achieves remarkable results on real-world datasets NTU-RGB+D and CMU Panoptic, surpassing the state-of-the-art in novel view video prediction, demonstrating significant gains in SSIM, PSNR, and FVD scores of 26.1%, 13.6%, and 60% respectively, without the use of prior views.

In this research, inter-orbital coupling was demonstrated using femtosecond laser writing, which enables orthogonal modes in a photonic lattice to couple with each other at different spatial locations. We characterized an asymmetric double-well structure, mapped its propagation dynamics and successfully created a device capable of spatial mode conversion anywhere within a photonic chip. Utilizing higher-order photonic mode phase structure, our experiment showed that a trimer configuration can serve as a $\pi$-phase grinder for interference-based metrology and quantum applications.

The Ω-baryon, which contains sss quarks and has only been marginally detected in past experiments, has primarily been studied using theoretical methods so far. A study aims to explore this particle's properties utilizing a quark model with linear confining forces. Calculated resonance masses are presented for the ground and excited states of S, P, D, and F quark systems. A linear nature of the Regge trajectory, supported by calculated data and magnetic moments, has also been examined. This study compares its results to other approaches and available experimental evidence.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In comparing our detailed model to a widely accepted 'well mixed' model, notable discrepancies in the distribution of aerosol particles became evident, with implications for our understanding of the spread of airborne pathogens. Furthermore, the differences identified in our study are expected to be relevant to a broader range of enclosed settings beyond urban buses.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with an adjacent layer. Researchers have primarily focused on situations where interfaces do not significantly affect spin-orbit coupling. In this study, we examine the influence of interfacial scattering within Bi/Co multilayers to determine spin-orbit coupling's spatial distribution. Using a combination of experimental measurements and theoretical modeling, we discovered that the magnitude of interfacial scattering relative to spin-orbit coupling can be a critical factor, leading to varied outcomes. In situations where interfacial scattering between layers is low, the spin-orbit coupling remains localized near the adjacent interface. Conversely, when scattering between layers is high, the spin-orbit coupling extends further, eventually exhibiting a linear relationship with layer thickness. This result is particularly notable in multilayer structures and may influence their overall properties at the interface, in addition to properties in the bulk.

This paper provides the quantum mechanics framework within the context of a fractional quantum system in $N$-dimensional space. We have achieved this goal by achieving exact solutions to the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation for a class of generalized Mie-type potential in $N$-dimensional space. We have based our approach on the Jumarie type fractional derivative definition, which enables us to deal with fractional complex power functions. Our results include the potential energy and wave function equations, from which we have obtained the corresponding boundary condition. We have then numericalized our results in three-dimensional, two-dimensional, and one-dimensional spaces.

We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimisation problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularisation. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance.

We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan ditau production and calculate precise corrections to this process, taking into account the effects of quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order. A specialized code is developed to efficiently generate these corrections, allowing for more accurate simulations of ditau events. By applying these simulations to recent LHC data, we can place constraints on a type of exotic particle, known as vector leptoquarks, based on their mass and coupling strength. This code is an important tool for ongoing and future searches for vector leptoquarks at the LHC, particularly those involving the collision of protons at high energies.

Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by transferring information from other medical imaging modalities, such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), through novel synthesis techniques. Nonetheless, the restricted capture of low-dose PET data available in clinical settings poses a significant challenge for these models, as they struggle with new, unknown scan parameters and protocols. To overcome this limitation, we developed an innovative framework that combines physics-based forward models and neural networks to produce high-quality PET images at standard doses while being resilient to various scan protocols, allowing the models to generalize to new protocols and protocols outside their training data. This approach leverages neural networks to incorporate uncertainty in their calculations and enhances robustness through the use of robust loss functions, as validated through numerous simulations and data sets. Furthermore, we demonstrated the efficacy of this method by applying it to various low-dose PET image reconstruction tasks, including brain, abdominal, and whole-body scans.

A linguistic analysis known as centering theory (CT) explains how coherence in conversations emerges from the connections between successive statements. This paper explores the link between CT and advanced computer systems that identify relationships within a text. By developing specific metrics and a search-based method, the study examines if modern computer systems that recognize connections within a text align with the principles of CT. The analysis indicates a correlation between the systems' ability to recognize connections and their ability to model the coherence of the text, but also reveals that these computer systems are not necessarily improved by considering the ideas underlying CT. Furthermore, the study finds that these computer systems already incorporate the coherence information required to recognize connections within the text, making CT's contribution limited. Additionally, the study discusses aspects that influence connections within the text but are not accounted for by CT, including the systems' knowledge and their tendency to favor more recent statements. By incorporating these elements, the study presents a revised version of CT and shows that it better captures the connections within the text compared to the original CT.

Recently, WiFi has become the primary method for locating individuals or devices within indoor settings. To facilitate this process, WiFi fingerprinting, a technique where reference measurements with known locations are collected and analyzed, has become a standard approach in positioning methods and algorithms discussed in academic literature. However, measuring spatial distances between these collected data sets, also known as WiFi fingerprints, relies heavily on the choice of signal distance metric employed to map signal intensity to geographical distance. To address this issue, the researchers proposed using machine learning to enhance the estimation of geospatial distances between these data sets. This research analyzed 13 diverse datasets from various open sources in order to create a universally applicable model suitable for a wide range of indoor environments. The novel approach developed extracted meaningful data features from a set of conventional signal distance metrics using feature selection and genetic algorithms. To demonstrate the versatility of this approach, models were tested on previously unused datasets from the training and validation stages. Furthermore, a comparative analysis was conducted among different machine learning algorithms utilizing a wide range of evaluation metrics, including their scalability to accommodate diverse real-world datasets.

The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by 2-4 factors or even more, depending on machine design parameters. Consequently, carefully selecting filling patterns can delay the onset of beam breakup, enhancing the potential applications of future energy recovery linacs.

To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering must be known. In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit and shown to be composed of a two-gluon CEV, allowing extraction of its universal components. By subtracting collinear divergent components in a $s$-channel limit approach, the two-gluon CEV was found to contribute 2 units to its eigenvalue in an all-color average, in addition to a color-stripped impact that can be compared to predictions from amplitude techniques, such as the maximum entropy method.

Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Although the 'end exclusion zone' concept has been successfully incorporated into models for cylindrical and spherical surfaces, its implications for curved surfaces with varied geometries have yet to be explored. In this study, we introduce a revised strong-stretching theory that applies to molten polymer brushes on curved surfaces of any complexity, identifying distinct regimes that give rise to end exclusion zones - including those with positive curvature and negative Gaussian curvature. By numerically solving the strong-stretching brush equations, we predict how the size of the end exclusion zone, chain end distribution, chain polarization, and free energy of stretching change with mean and Gaussian curvatures, offering a detailed understanding of how surface curvature affects brush geometry and free energy calculations. This comprehensive knowledge can be utilized to simulate a broad range of brush geometries encountered in the assembly of block copolymer melts.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph.

Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporally varying sources, like blazars, which change significantly over a year. Despite this limitation, this approach shows promise for automatically identifying these sources and detecting transient phenomena and giant structures often missed in focused observations.

Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We establish theoretical bounds on achievable social welfare when employing a query-based approach and find that this results in a marginally improved approximation of optimal social welfare when considering a general scenario. However, when combinatorial optimization domains are in question, we demonstrate the ability to obtain high-quality approximations, achieving a $2$-approximation when applying it to specific optimization tasks including graph matching, arborescence in directed graphs, and Boolean satisfiability. We also examine issues of honesty and provide ways in which some of our solutions can be implemented fairly with incentives based on payment schemes such as the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves method. We propose and evaluate a new metric, the price of serial dictatorship, offering a quantitative indicator of the efficacy of combinatorial optimization solutions obtained via action sequences.

We designed two distinct point spread function (PSF) analysis techniques 
for detecting wide binary asteroids within wide field surveys, and subsequently
applied these to Pan-STARRS1 images featuring main belt asteroids spanning 
4 to 60 kilometers in diameter. As existing records, cited in Johnston (2019),
reveal less than 10 documented binary asteroids within this size range, with
orbital separations exceeding 10% of their primary components' Hill radius, it is 
essential to discover additional wide binary asteroids to clarify binary
stability constraints and enhance asteroid mass comprehension. Our analytical 
process for each image involved two approaches: firstly, by correlating the 
orientation of the asteroid's elliptical PSF with its sidereal motion across 
the sky, and secondly, by creating a one-dimensional profile from collapsing the 
image along the asteroid's trajectory, and comparing it to that of nearby field 
stars. Any marked deviations from typical measurements of single asteroids 
were identified and flagged; among these flagged targets, the most notable were 
designated binary prospects awaiting confirmation through high-resolution 
imaging.

This research supplements the findings related to the specified context, model, and estimation methods initially presented by Auerbach in 2019. The paper explores the link between social connections and academic achievement based on a large dataset involving over 7,000 students in South Korea. It also investigates the relationship between a student's academic achievement and the achievements of their closest friends within the same dataset. A two-step estimation approach is employed to analyze the data, with the first step involving the estimation of a linear regression model and the second step involving the estimation of a logistic regression model.

This study introduces novel versions of the Leibniz Rule for the Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order fractional integral and derivative. It derives key formulas, including product, quotient, and chain rules for both the integral and differential operators. Specifically, four distinct product rule formulas, four quotient rule formulas derived from product rule types, and four chain rule formulas have been established.

We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context.

The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models. By applying graph theory and computational algorithms, a study analyzes the spatial structures of 849 heteroknot proteins to determine their fundamental topological characteristics. The findings reveal a uniform distribution of 2-loop knots and a more complex distribution of nested loop knots. The research shows that heteroknot proteins can be distinguished from one-loop knots and nested one-loop knots based on their energy profiles. By correlating the spatial structures with energy profiles, the study uncovers various folding pathways for heteroknot proteins in their native state. The approach is versatile and can be used to study other complex protein structures, including cross-knotted and double-stranded knotted proteins. The study's approach is an important step in using topological properties to predict the complex folding processes of knotted proteins.

Let $\omega$ be a Kaehler form on the real $4$-dimensional torus $T^4$. Given that it fulfills an irrationality criterion which can be realized via an arbitrarily minor adjustment of $\omega$, this note proves that the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group of the one-point symplectic blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is countably infinite.

A detailed investigation of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem has been undertaken with an emphasis on its underlying mathematical structures drawn from Lie algebras, geometry, and number theory. The principles behind the anomalous NG theorem have been explored using both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups. In analyzing this phenomenon, a quasi-Heisenberg algebra was discovered in a variety of symmetry breaking scenarios associated with the anomalous NG theorem. Notably, this algebraic structure can cause deviations from the conventional Heisenberg uncertainty principle, which could potentially be experimentally verified. A framework for effective potential formalism was developed to better understand the mechanisms driving the anomalous NG theorem. A study of a bosonic kaon condensation model incorporating a fermion's nonrelativistic sector using an effective potential approach was conducted. A finding of this research is that there is no restriction on the number of long-lived Nambu-Goldstone bosons resulting from the breaking of a continuous global symmetry within a relativistic quantum field theory.

Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and versatile models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised methods. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a general-purpose language model to generate phrasal alterations, while a task-specific instructor model culls high-quality examples from the generated pool. We demonstrate that employing this counterfactual data in learning yields a relatively small model that achieves comparable performance to a fully trained large model on SQuAD and CMU Movie Dialogue Corpus, while exhibiting improved causal robustness. Moreover, we show that such a model is capable of extending to new counterfactual data types with minimal supplementary training.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. To explore remote epitaxy, our study delves into growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on graphene-covered sapphire substrates with varying levels of cleanliness. Our findings indicate that even on extremely clean graphsene, the Heusler compound prefers van der Waals epitaxy rather than remote epitaxy, forming closed structures that seal the graphene from pinhole defects during annealing. Extremely pure graphene with few defects does not significantly impact the Heusler's structure or magnetic properties.

A code is referred to as $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear if it results from a particular type of encoding process called the Gray image of a code that has properties derived from $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-additive code for a prime number p greater than two. In this study, specific aspects of these $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes, particularly the dimension and the number of zeros in the code, are explored and formulas are provided to calculate these values.

Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates a new setting called the single positive scenario, in which each piece of data is marked by only a single relevant label without any additional information regarding potential irrelevant labels.  A novel technique known as single-to-multi-label sampling was developed to generate multi-label data based on this single positive label annotation.  This new approach is a supplemental tool that allows current unconditional and conditional GANs to generate high-quality multi-label data while significantly reducing the required annotation. Experimental findings with real image datasets demonstrate that the technique can effectively produce accurate multi-label data even in comparison to a model trained using comprehensive datasets.

The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through an abstract adjoint relationship, capturing fundamental aspects of the algebra's underlying properties. This abstract adjoint relationship must be seen within the context of weakly natural transformations, a concept that arises from categorifying functors. This formulation of the relationship provides the basis for interpreting the inherent mathematical structure in physical terms.

The cause behind gamma-rays in nearby galaxies emitting high energy radiation remains a mystery.  Hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes, formed when magnetic fields reconnect, could provide a potential explanation.  By applying this "MAD" model to the 15 most radiant galaxies, we found that it can account for gamma-rays in the energy band if the matter falling into the black hole occurs at a rate that's just a tiny fraction of its potential.  However, at higher accretion rates, absorption from the abundant low-energy photons hinders the gamma-rays, thwarting the model's explanation.  Moreover, using an alternate approach to describe magnetic field interactions with electrons also led to similar results, albeit with a slightly broader range of accretion rates.  When comparing these models to actual data from the Cherenkov Telescope Array simulations, we found they can yield similar results, but with a marked difference in the spectral shape of gamma-rays.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, this study investigates the development of effective methods to analyze cardiac auscultation sounds that have been affected by both types of distortions.  A comparison of different signal representation techniques, specifically time-domain, frequency-domain, time-frequency domain, and morphological signal processing methods was conducted to determine their effectiveness in distinguishing normal heart sounds from abnormal ones in noisy conditions.  The study used a large dataset featuring diverse recording devices and included noise and clean sounds.  The results showed that the time-frequency domain and morphological signal processing methods significantly outperformed other techniques.  Time-frequency domain methods achieved the best overall performance, with an accuracy of 94.5% in a noisy environment.  The findings are expected to be beneficial for creating effective, portable devices for cardiac auscultation without the need for sophisticated noise-reduction technologies.

The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. This paper proposes FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare designed to address these difficulties. FedHealth aggregates data via federated learning and employs transfer learning to develop personalized models. It succeeds in providing accurate, personalized healthcare without compromising security and data confidentiality. Experimentation reveals that FedHealth yields 5.3% greater accuracy in wearable activity recognition when compared to conventional approaches. Furthermore, FedHealth demonstrates versatility, extensibility, and vast potential applications in the healthcare industry.

This study classifies portfolio optimization strategies with higher order moments including skewness and kurtosis to aid Hedge Fund practitioners in navigating various paradigms and methodologies. Key research approaches, such as utility theory and multi-objective optimization, are reviewed, with an examination of their benefits and limitations.

In large-scale organizations, recruiting involves interviewing a substantial number of applicants, a time-consuming and intricate process. To achieve efficiency, a well-planned approach to selection is crucial. This process comprises multiple, interconnected problems, each mirroring a well-known computational issue. While individual research has been extensively conducted, an integrated examination of these problems is uncommon. This paper addresses two critical aspects of application processing: creating review and interview panels and scheduling interviews. We developed a prototype system to automate interview planning for a real-world scenario. Compared to existing, manual methods, our approach yields a superior plan. To achieve this, we evaluated different algorithmic options and tailored them to solve panel creation and scheduling issues. We experimented with these solutions using real data, presenting our findings. This study may serve as a starting point for further development aimed at fully automating application processing processes.

This study tackles a complex control issue, characterized by the existence of multiple, evolving costs that obstruct optimization efforts. Unlike similar problems in the field, where costs are shown to be naturally well-structured and ordered, the problem at hand involves unbounded cost evolution. To overcome this challenge, researchers have successively refined the problem's formulation to ultimately achieve a controlled reflection process as its solution. A key aspect of this work involves demonstrating the efficiency of its problem-solving approach by comparing it to an alternative, more conventional method.

To explore the significance of new physics, our research investigates asymmetric leptoquark pair creation in the Large Hadron Collider to provide solid constraints on its properties and aid in identifying its potential. Asymmetric production stands out from conventional methods as leptoquarks created in proton-proton collisions aren't opposite charges. To make this process possible, we outline the required conditions and list all relevant combinations of leptoquark groups that can create it. Furthermore, our studies in the Standard Model and its scalar extensions demonstrate how to integrate this process into reinterpretations of existing experiments, producing more accurate leptoquark property constraints.

We analyzed a sample of 106 galaxies for which data is available for two specific fine structure lines of neutral atomic carbon, and we found their average conditions to be significantly non-equilibrium. Based on exact solutions of a 3-level system without any assumptions regarding hydrogen gas properties, we found the line formation mechanism to be influenced by non-LTE (local thermodynamic equilibrium) excitation. This non-equilibrium state may explain recent observations of gas temperatures around 25K and is not correlated with actual gas temperatures. It also hampers our ability to estimate molecular gas temperatures based on carbon isotope lines and contributes uncertainty in the mass estimates of molecular gas. However, this line ratio is valuable in modeling both CO and CI spectra and is independent of radiative transfer models. It is also proposed that extreme starbursts with low line ratios and high dust temperatures could be associated with massive low-density winds and post-merger galaxies with retained massive reservoirs.

Levenshtein initially introduced the sequence reconstruction problem in 2001.
It deals with a scenario in which the same sequence from a specific set undergoes
different channel transmissions and the results are obtained through measurements,
as shown in Figure 1. These measurements yield a set of strings that were obtained
through distinct distortions during the transmission process. It is assumed that the
original sequence was changed at most a certain number of times, denoted by $d$.
The task at hand involves using the measurement outcomes to determine the original sequence.
It can be viewed as a $d$-distorted version of the classical problem of finding the original sequence
from measurements in Figure 1, without any time constraints.
In this research, the focus is on the version of the problem that has a time constraint
and is defined as follows: given a collection of strings that were obtained through distinct
distortions during the transmission process and a time constraint $\tau$, determine the original sequence
that likely produced the measurement outcomes, with the restriction that the number of changes to the original sequence did not exceed $d$ during the transmission process.
The research also compares an existing lower bound from 2010 of 2d+1 for the number of strings
in the measurement outcomes that are necessary to correctly solve the problem with the time constraint
for the scenario in which the original sequence was changed at most a certain number of times, denoted by $d$, during the transmission process.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual supermassive black hole binaries moving in highly elliptical orbits. By comparing various methods for computing PTA signals from these binaries, our findings indicate that employing approximate analytic expressions yields the most efficient computation, leading to a significant reduction of up to 50 times in computational costs compared to other methods. The accuracy of these analytic expressions is validated through a relevant mismatch metric and found to be sufficiently precise for the PTA parameter space of interest. Furthermore, we introduce an improved approach using spline interpolation to enhance computation speeds by an additional factor of up to 3 times. The implementation of this method is part of the $E\text{PICMC}$ suite.

We establish that in ASEP, a system with initial data represented by discrete steps, a second-class particle placed at the origin, will asymptotically converge to a velocity whose probability distribution is uniform across the interval $[-1,1]$ as time tends to infinity. This conclusive finding addresses two unresolved conjectures from "The TASEP speed process" and enables us to develop the ASEP speed process.

This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods for model compartment analysis. A unified framework emerges, emphasizing the critical role that context, drawing from epidemiology, medicine, and biology, plays in informing both model development and analysis. Failing to consider the biological implications of mathematical models during data fitting risks producing statistically significant results, but lacking practical significance for guiding pandemic management, mitigation, and eventual control.

We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent atom-molecule conversion in systems with one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions, we found that the interplay between collisions that transfer spin and light-based association results in stable atom-molecule pair formation from initial spinless atoms through two-body interactions equivalent to an effective three-body recombination. In our study, we also investigate the impact of light-based association and initial magnetization when a precise condition is met. Furthermore, we explored two scenarios: one in which the dark state condition is met imperfectly, either generally known as the adiabatic case, or not at all. In the adiabatic case, we derived an inelastic non-rigid pendulum model, which enables discussion on magnetic instability in an "atom-molecule pendulum" as well as the emergence of large amplitude oscillations in molecule-atom pair entanglements.

Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data items identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture multiple items at any given level can be linked to unlimited numbers of items across all levels. Additionally, as there are an abundance of available primer pairs, we can organize data in a highly multi-level hierarchy. Furthermore, as the current write operation in our system can target any location within the range of a read operation, we can perform a write operation on any level without restriction, making it possible to create a wide range of data configurations including those with a large distance between the head and tail. As a result of these benefits, our system exhibits superior performance when compared to the existing DNA-storage technologies. Specifically, it outperforms the state-of-the-art technology by as much as 6 times in terms of write-operation efficiency and 7 times in terms of total-data-storage efficiency.

Our proposed model utilizes the physics-based shallow water equations as a foundation, modifying them to include an artificial neural network in place of the viscosity term. By doing so, we derive an analytical expression for the neural network's output, which is subsequently used to modify the equations. The resulting model tracks the viscosity term over time and includes a numerical scheme to solve the spatial and temporal components of the equations. Our data-driven approach leverages the Lagrange method and the adjoint technique to obtain an analytical expression for the neural network's output, which is then tracked over time. We validate our model against real-world data and observe a significant improvement in its performance.

HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at various exposure levels
to counterbalance digital cameras' limited dynamic range. This research presents a
technique for automatically determining optimal exposure settings for smartphone
images by utilizing the camera's inherent characteristics. Furthermore, an innovative
image fusion method is introduced, leveraging optimization and weighted averages.
These techniques are applied to a mobile HDR application, demonstrating the
feasibility of the approach. Comparative assessments are also conducted to
demonstrate the introduced solution's efficiency and effectiveness in comparison to
established methods.

Causal deep learning, an emerging and significant area within the broader field of machine learning, aims to integrate causal knowledge into deep learning models through a flexible representation framework. This will lead to more accurate and generalizable predictions and inferences, though significant hurdles remain due to the diverse nature of methods within the field. A new publication addresses this challenge by categorizing methods within causal deep learning, refining Pearl's causal hierarchy while considering parametric assumptions and input/representation structures. The resulting framework provides researchers with a map for benchmarking, comparing methods, and identifying knowledge gaps across machine learning disciplines, such as supervised learning, reinforcement learning, and generative modeling. The authors open-source this framework for the research community to use, with potential applications in guiding related work sections and highlighting paper contributions.

This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle, and is nearly equivalent to the set of oriented submersions in 2 dimensions. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is derivable from a specific application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions, combined with the findings from Harer's stability theorem and Miller and Morita's work.

This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods on
high-performance computers for models of cardiac mechanics with molecular motor dynamics.
Cardiac mechanics models typically rely on solving identically shaped problems with
differentiated material properties across small subdomains.
We tested various multilevel preconditioning strategies for this type of problem and
found that an optimal BDDC implementation with multiple smoothing levels of AMG in
each subdomain and on the coarse grid can significantly outperform other methods,
particularly when comparing to an idealized BDDC implementation used as a reference.

Standard models of diffusion fail when describing the motion of certain particles, such as polymers and stock prices, due to their tendency to exhibit unusual behavior. In an attempt to improve the description of these phenomena, we have developed a probabilistic model based on the concept of fractional moments, which can be linked to the Levy distribution and accurately predicts the outcomes of random processes like the geometric Brownian motion and other processes that are commonly used in mathematics and finance. By applying our model, we have obtained precise formulas to calculate the probability of particles moving beyond certain distances, as well as their expected travel times, which can be compared to existing theoretical predictions through numerical methods.

A fundamental theory is developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between the modes of dielectric optical resonators, with the framework being applicable across various geometries and modes. The general approach allows for a wide range of phenomena resulting from linear interactions, scattering, and Kerr nonlinearity, such as mode coupling and phase modulation, to be analyzed. The developed theory is specifically applied to a waveguide with a microresonator in close proximity, enabling the computation of mode coupling and phase modulation terms. Furthermore, a dimensionless equation is derived to describe the dynamics of two identical counterpropagating modes in a loop resonator and, under the condition of mode identity, it is proven that cross-phase modulation is precisely twice as strong as self-phase modulation.

A recent study proposes a novel deep learning framework that utilizes generative adversarial networks to generate highly detailed turbulent velocity patterns from limited-resolution data across a range of Reynolds numbers. A specially designed multiscale model was utilized to create a high-resolution velocity pattern from a low-resolution pattern with corresponding flow characteristics. This pattern was then fed into a global generator network that produces a highly detailed velocity pattern at the desired resolution. Validation of the proposed method showed that it accurately replicates turbulent velocity patterns from two low-resolution data sets with different resolutions, as measured by the mean squared error. Furthermore, it successfully recreated two low-resolution velocity patterns from a single trained generator network. A key finding of this study is that it demonstrates the ability to recognize complex patterns in turbulent flows across a wide range of Reynolds numbers. A key limitation of the proposed method is that it does not account for boundary conditions. To address this limitation, the method was applied to three low-resolution velocity patterns with different boundary conditions, and it successfully recreated them without prior knowledge of these conditions.

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems. A key challenge is ensuring that the learned knowledge is retained and adapted effectively without significant setbacks. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on reinforcement learning methods that can handle continuous knowledge updates. However, evaluating and comparing these methods is difficult due to the lack of standardized testing tools. To address this issue, we present L2Explorer, a cutting-edge software environment designed to manage and conduct experiments on continuous learning reinforcement learning scenarios. L2Explorer is distinguished from similar platforms by its ability to manage large-scale, systematically varied experiments on a wide range of reinforcement learning methods and environments. In our testing of the software, we conducted an extensive set of experiments on continuous learning scenarios using a combination of custom-generated data and widely recognized benchmarks. Our findings, which we report in detail, demonstrate the benefits of utilizing continuous learning reinforcement learning methods, as well as the potential drawbacks of various widely used methods, including the onset of excessive exploration caused by changes in the environment.

Understanding business processes relies on process discovery methods, analyzing data trails to reveal underlying processes. As processes evolve over time, their corresponding models must adapt, otherwise they may inaccurately predict future behaviors. Our approach develops an algorithm to identify processes from event flows, represented as Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graphs, providing temporal process data and subsequently declarative process models. We validate this method through experiments and analyses, comparing it against changing real processes to ensure its effectiveness and accuracy. Our approach and associated test data are available online.
This note provides an introduction to the interplay between Hodge-theoretic and geometric approaches to compactifying moduli spaces of algebraic varieties.

Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are more likely to exhibit redder NUV$-r$ colors even when considering factors like bulge-to-total mass ratio and stellar mass. This indicates a stronger relationship between star formation within massive early-type galaxies and their intrinsic mass density than with their bulge-to-total mass density.
